evidence.field: 字源字形 / 說文解字 / 書證
evidence.text: The entry identifies 口 as a pictograph of the human mouth, gives the Shuowen definition “人所以言食也。象形。凡口之屬皆从口”, and lists oracle-bone instances (including 甲1193 and 甲1215), late Shang bronze examples, Chu manuscript, Shuowen seal, Qin slips, and clerical forms. It separately records the mouth sense and later/other senses such as passage, population, speech, blade edge, and rim; its gloss list does not establish the chronology or semantic derivation of those extensions.
evidence.title: 口 kǒu - 漢典

evidence.field: 說文原文 / 字形演變
evidence.text: The page transcribes Xu Shen’s account: “人所以言食也。象形。凡口之屬皆从口。” Its displayed sequence identifies examples as oracle-bone 甲1215 and 甲1277, late Shang bronze 四祀弋其卣, Chu manuscript 郭.忠.5, Shuowen seal, Qin and Han clerical forms. This supports a usable explanatory sequence, but the page is a transcription/index, not visual examination of the underlying inscriptions.
evidence.title: 说文解字：口

evidence.source: 小學堂文字學資料庫 guide
evidence.text: The guide describes a collaborative database of oracle-bone, bronze, Warring States, seal and regular-script forms. It explicitly states that glyph images and glyph-attribute information obtained through the query interface are dedicated under CC0 1.0 where legally permitted. This makes a narrowly scoped, versioned 口 extract plausible for repeatable local validation, provided the exported records retain identifiers and scope.
evidence.title: 小學堂新手入門

evidence.source: Wikimedia Commons file description; source linked to 小學堂 record
evidence.text: The description page identifies the image as a Shang oracle-script rendering of 口, names Sinica Database record 41.E513 and notes 甲1193, and states CC0 1.0/public-domain reuse. The Commons page contains an inspected direct “Original file” link to the SVG, unlike the previously failed guessed shard URL. It is an explanatory redraw attributed to a database glyph record, not a photograph or a direct facsimile of the original bone.
evidence.title: File:口-oracle.svg - Wikimedia Commons

evidence.text: The inspected database landing page identifies its institutional maintainers and states that its current corpus contains 2,548 oracle-bone head characters and 24,701 glyph records (as of 2026-09-27). The landing page did not expose a directly readable character-specific 口 record during this inspection; the Commons description supplies the verified record identifier and direct character-page link.
evidence.title: 小學堂甲骨文

evidence.field: 康熙字典 / 國語辭典書證
evidence.text: The entry quotes the Shuowen description, cites 易·頤卦 “自求口食” and 書·大禹謨 “唯口出好興戎”, and gives a Han-period citation from 論衡·道虛 for an object's opening, alongside 《孟子·梁惠王上》 for household population. These demonstrate documented uses, but this modern page does not date the underlying texts precisely or establish when each extended sense arose.

gaps: The Sinica character-specific page linked from Commons (record 41.E513 / 甲1193) was not opened and independently inspected; Commons’ description page itself was accessible and provided a verified click-through link and source identifier.
No original inscription image was visually inspected in this research pass. Use the Commons oracle redraw only as an explanatory glyph, explicitly labelled as a modern redraw based on Sinica data.

The current Sinica guide explicitly permits CC0 reuse of glyph images and glyph-attribute information, but no versioned export was made. A small extract scoped to 口’s linked oracle, bronze, Chu, seal and Qin/Han forms could improve repeatable validation; version and hash remain unrecorded, so do not claim an extract exists.

Shuowen’s pictographic analysis is consistent with the dictionary’s listed early examples, but the precise graphic changes between individual inscriptions are not established by inspected image evidence. No corruption hypothesis or competing formation analysis was supported by these inspected pages.

The dictionary’s cited traditional texts provide separate examples of mouth, speech, household population and openings; they do not establish a dated semantic chain. The exact earliest attestation of each extended sense remains open.
This research did not establish an independent chronology for senses meaning entrance/opening, population, blade edge, or rim, and does not infer one from the modern dictionary’s sense ordering.
